To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the antigenic potentials of heat shock proteins (Hsp) are higher in malaria than in other diseases.
HSP90 was a major target of antibody response in malaria patients and in non-lethal P. yoelii infected mice.
HSP90 is the most immunodominant antigen among the three major HSPs, HSP90, HSP70, and HSP65, in malaria infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of antibodies to HSPs in malaria.
the role of antibodies to HSPs in the host immune response to malaria infection.
the potential of HSPs in the development of a malaria vaccine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HSPs are immunogenic and that HSPs, particularly HSP90, are potential candidates as a target of the host immune system for malaria infection.
the HSPs are immunogenic in malaria infection.
HSP90 is an immunodominant antigen recognized by the host in malaria infection, while HSP70 and 65 are also immunogenic but less than HSP90.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HSPs are immunodominants in malaria infection and that the anti-HSP90 antibodies are most elevated.
HSP90, HSP70 and, to a lesser extent, HSP65, are recognized by the host antibody response in malaria infection.
the HSP90-specific antibodies are a potential marker for malaria infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HSP90 may be a potential candidate antigen for malaria vaccine development.
HSPs are potential targets of the host immune response in malaria infection.
the antigenicity of HSP90 may be higher than those of the other heat shock proteins in malaria.
